You can check out at any time. More info Join us on WhatsApp New bathing water test results have been released and show there are five European countries where you would not want to go swimming in some seas or open waters. The European Environment Agency (EEA) has released its annual report into the quality of bathing waters across the continent. The report found 100% of the bathing waters around Cyprus meet the required standard for swimming, with Greece, Bulgaria and Austria also reaching the top of the charts. But Albania, which sits opposite Italy on the Adriatic Sea and is to the north of Greece on the Ionian Sea, was at the other end of the chart. L ess than 16% of bathing waters in Albania are rated excellent and 23% are 'poor' - with significant levels of faecal bacteria, according to Which? Albania has become increasingly popular as a holiday destination thanks to long beaches and cheap accommodation. Just under 1million UK tourists visit Albania annually, making the UK one of the strongest growing source markets for the country's surging tourism sector. British travel to the destination has spiked significantly in recent years due to low-cost direct flights from UK airports and favorable exchange rates Other countries with poor results are Estonia, Poland and the landlocked nation of Hungary. All had less than 65% of their bathing waters rated excellent. Belgium also managed just 67.9% hitting the minimum standards. While Hungary has no sea coast, it is home to the largest freshwater lake in Europe - Lake Balaton covers 600sq km and has 200 sq km of coastline. Lake Balaton’s water is officially rated as excellent for bathing and is regularly monitored. However, because of its shallow depth and high plankton and mineral content, the water is naturally cloudy rather than crystal clear. The EEA has an interactive map where you can check if a beach or lake meets the EU standards. Story Saved You can find this story in My Bookmarks. Or by navigating to the user icon in the top right. https://www.dw.com/en/cargo-ship-with-10.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5K7Nh Turkish search crews found a life boat with no people on board Image: x.com/denizcilikgm Advertisement Turkish authorities are searching for 10 people aboard a cargo ship that sank after a collision with another vessel in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul early Wednesday. "We believe, and have more or less confirmed, that the Tugberk Imamoglu has sunk," Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu told reporters in Istanbul. Uraloglu said all 10 crew members aboard the vessel were Turkish nationals and that attempts to reach them by mobile phone had been unsuccessful. "We can say that the sinking occurred rapidly in 11 minutes. No one has been found alive," he added. The bulk carrier Tugberk Imamoglu and the chemical tanker Alsu collided at around 3 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) off the city's western Silivri district, the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement. Two helicopters and 12 search and rescue vessels are scouring the area. The Transport Ministry's maritime directorate said that life-saving equipment, including a lifeboat belonging to the Tugberk Imamoglu , had been found floating on the surface. "Unfortunately, the crew members were not inside," it added. The 90-meter (295-foot) cargo ship Tugberk Imamoglu, built in 1990, was traveling from Turkey’s Iskenderun to Eregli in the Black Sea Image: DHA What else do we know about the missing ship? The 90-meter (295-foot) Turkish -flagged bulk carrier was en route to the Black Sea ​port ‌of Eregli from Iskenderun when the collision happened. According to the maritime directorate, it was carrying 4,200 tons of rolled steel. Authorities believe it sank in waters around 900 meters deep. The 91-meter Turkish-flagged Alsu , was sailing from Kocaeli, east of Istanbul, to the Aegean port of Aliaga. It was empty at the time of the collision and did not appear to have suffered any damage, the governor's office said. The Sea of Marmara forms part of one of the world's busiest shipping corridors, linking the Mediterranean to the Black Sea via the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits. https://www.politico.eu/article/en-europ.text: BRUXELLES — L’Union européenne devrait obliger les géants de la tech à investir dans l’approvisionnement en énergie propre afin de répondre aux besoins croissants en électricité de leurs centres de données, a estimé auprès de POLITICO la vice-présidente exécutive de la Commission européenne chargée de la Transition propre, juste et compétitive. Teresa Ribera a averti que les infrastructures très gourmandes en électricité qui alimentent l’intelligence artificielle mettent de plus en plus à rude épreuve les réseaux électriques, entraînant une concurrence acharnée pour l’énergie et risquant de faire grimper les factures. “Ça a été un choc, et ça se passe à un rythme effréné, a-t-elle retracé. En 2022, alors que nous cherchions à déterminer comment passer à une énergie entièrement électrique et propre, nous n’avions pas prévu une telle augmentation supplémentaire de la demande en électricité [...] et quelle que soit la rapidité avec laquelle nous planifions les réseaux et les nouvelles capacités d’énergie verte, la demande augmente à un rythme effréné. Cela crée donc certaines tensions.” Advertisement Advertisement Selon l’Espagnole, les gouvernements ont trois options : ne rien faire et prendre le risque de voir s’aggraver les tensions économiques et sociales parce que “les prix ne cessent d’augmenter” en raison de la hausse de la demande ; imposer un moratoire sur la construction de centres de données, comme c’est le cas dans certaines régions des Etats-Unis ; ou obliger les opérateurs à produire leur propre énergie. Selon elle, les géants de la tech ont les moyens d’envisager cette troisième option. “Les entreprises à l’origine de cette activité [...] concentrent un pouvoir de marché et des capacités d’une ampleur sans précédent. On peut donc, pour parler sans détour, leur demander d’investir dans ce dont elles pourraient avoir besoin et de veiller à ce que cela évite de nouveaux conflits avec les populations locales”, a-t-elle défendu lors de l’interview. Lorsqu’on lui a demandé si l’UE devrait obliger les Big Tech à financer eux-mêmes leur approvisionnement en énergie propre, Teresa Ribera a répondu : “Je pense que nous devrions le faire.” Ces déclarations interviennent alors que la Commission continue de travailler à l’élaboration de nouvelles normes d’efficacité énergétique pour les datacenters . Le commissaire européen à l’Energie, Dan Jørgensen, avait insisté fin mai sur le fait que les entreprises souhaitant construire des centres de données en Europe devaient s’engager à respecter les objectifs climatiques et énergétiques du continent. A l’inverse, le président de l’European Data Centre Association (EDCA), Lex Coors, s’est inscrit en faux en juin, déclarant à POLITICO que l’Europe devait donner la priorité à l’intelligence artificielle plutôt qu’à ses ambitions climatiques immédiates, sous peine de céder sa souveraineté technologique à la Chine. Advertisement Advertisement Reste que les gouvernements européens se démènent aussi pour gérer la forte hausse de la demande énergétique des infrastructures d’IA et éviter une augmentation des émissions de gaz à effet de serre due à leur consommation d’énergie. A la fin de l’année dernière, l’Irlande a levé le moratoire sur les nouvelles constructions, à condition que les nouveaux datacenters disposent sur place de sources d’énergies renouvelables pour s’alimenter. Teresa Ribera a évoqué un projet de décret dévoilé le mois dernier par le gouvernement espagnol, qui imposerait aux centres de données de s’approvisionner à hauteur de 80% en électricité provenant d’installations éoliennes et solaires récentes, soit via une production sur site, soit en signant des contrats d’achat d’électricité à long terme (PPA) issue exclusivement d’énergies renouvelables. Mais elle a averti que ces PPA risquent de créer des tensions avec les autres consommateurs : “Si ces datacenters [...] signent des PPA avec des fournisseurs d’électricité, cette [énergie] constitue leur principale matière première et ils peuvent payer des prix plus élevés que ceux que notre industrie de base électro-intensive est en mesure de payer.” Et l’Espagnole d’ajouter : “Le développement de nouvelles capacités de production d’électricité prend du temps. Cela pourrait donc avoir des répercussions non seulement en matière de durabilité, si cela [entraînait], par exemple, un retard dans la sortie progressive du charbon, mais aussi en matière de concurrence équitable ou de compétitivité pour nos industries lors de la production de biens.” Compte tenu du développement rapide de l’IA et du nombre de centres de données cherchant à se raccorder au réseau en Europe, les autorités doivent agir rapidement pour mettre en place une réglementation, a plaidé Teresa Ribera. “On parle de mois, a-t-elle souligné. On ne parle pas de décennies, et probablement même pas d’années.” Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon. https://en.tempo.co/read/2118991/un-appr.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - A yearslong push to change the default view of the Earth came to a vote at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday with 164 countries in favor of a new map, the United States against it and six abstentions.Known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection, the map "offers a more accurate representation of the sizes of continental landmasses and to this end is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world," according to the resolution, which was spearheaded by several African countries.Togo's foreign minister, Robert Dussey, told the UN maps "shape our understanding of the world.""They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions," he said. "They are, therefore, never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation."No, Greenland is nowhere near as big as AfricaThe resolution pushes for countries to adopt the Equal Earth projection rather than the traditional Mercator projection, which was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.The Mercator projection accurately depicts the shapes and angles of landmasses, necessary for shipping, but distorts their relative sizes: landmasses near the Earth's poles appear larger while those near the equator look smaller. This makes Greenland appear about as big as Africa, despite the African continent being about 14 times larger.Togo's Dussey said his country aims to replace the maps used in its schools by the end of the year.The Mercator projection's use is a result of colonization, Dussey said, adding, "The world is changing. Africa also is changing."US, China, India, Japan, Mexico and part of EU fit in AfricaFrance, which co-sponsored the resolution, said on Friday that it would also abandon the Mercator projection.In that projection, "the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia," while "Greenland appears almost as big as Africa," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in statement."Changing maps obviously doesn't change the world," he acknowledged. "But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth."In support of the new projection, online campaign group #CorrectTheMap said, "You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare."The UN General Assembly vote is not legally binding and "in no way challenges the use of Mercator projection for maritime and aerial navigation, for which it remains fully suited," the ministry said in a statement.Equal Earth a 'distraction,' US saysAs the only country to vote against the resolution, the United States said the Equal Earth projection pushed an "ideological agenda" and distracted attention from "genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations.""Instead of focusing on genuine problems... this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice," US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote.Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Morocco, Serbia and Ukraine abstained from voting on the resolution.Read: How Climate Change is Reshaping Africa's Malaria RiskClick here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News

Photograph: Joanna Kordina/AAP Helen Haines Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack Independent MP now serious but stable, according to update from Melbourne’s Alfred hospital Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Adeshola Ore Fri 23 Oct 2026 20.41 EDT Last modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 21.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Independent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon. The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning. “The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said. Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries. The MP’s husband, Phil Haines, provided an update at the Alfred hospital on Wednesday, saying “both her heart and her mind are in good shape .” “I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind,” he said. “Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.” The alleged attack on Helen Haines shocked the nation. It shouldn’t have Read more Police on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Nugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail. On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday. “What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read. “As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.” Haines’ staff said they had been overwhelmed with kindness shown by the local community in Indi and across Australia and the globe. They said more than $730,000 had been raised for Save the Children in Haines’ honour after her husband directed people to donate to the special appeal as his wife recovered. “We are deeply moved by the extraordinary generosity of so many people,” the post read. The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about the temperature of political debat, security risks for MPs and mental health services in regional Victoria. WA Police charged a 56-year-old man after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the the state’s local government minister, Hannah Beazley, days after the alleged attack on Haines. A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack. Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/30/iran.text: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday, Oct. 30, that three oil tankers had encountered incidents while attempting to navigate routes Tehran considers unauthorized in the eastern and western sections of the Strait of Hormuz. All vessels were subsequently stopped in the waterway’s southern waters.According to Iranian state media, the Guard claimed the tankers had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and were attempting to leave the strait through routes opposed by Tehran, with the support of the U.S. military.The Guard said the vessels continued sailing despite repeated radio warnings before encountering trouble in what it described as unsafe areas.It provided no details about the tankers’ identities, their flags, the precise cause of the incidents or the condition of their crews.The reports came as Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday to continue efforts to broker an agreement between Iran and the United States.Uncertainty over the number of tankers damagedIn a separate incident whose possible connection to the Guard’s claims remains unclear, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, or UKMTO, reported that a small boat approached an oil tanker Thursday evening and attached two explosive devices to its hull above the waterline.The devices detonated, sparking a fire in the engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel.The Financial Times identified the tanker as the Louise 1.The incident occurred about 25 nautical miles (46 kilometers) northeast of Khasab, Oman.UKMTO said the fire had been extinguished, all crew members were safe and no environmental pollution had been reported. The tanker subsequently resumed its voyage toward its next port.The attack appeared to mark the first reported successful use of limpet mines against a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz since the U.S.-Iran war began in February 2026.It was not immediately clear who was responsible or whether the attack was connected to the Guard’s latest claims involving two tankers.Separately, Oman’s Maritime Security Center reported Friday that the Royal Navy of Oman had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged commercial vessel that came under attack and caught fire about 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam.The center said the crew members received necessary medical care but did not identify the vessel or those responsible for the attack.It remained unclear whether the incident was connected to other reported attacks on tankers in the strait.The Guard’s latest statements followed claims Thursday, Oct. 29, that three tankers had struck naval mines along the strait’s southern route, triggering explosions and fires.Iran’s regular military also reported Thursday that another tanker had caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.According to Agence France-Presse, Iranian officials claimed that all four vessels had been operating in prohibited and unsafe areas.However, it remained unclear whether the two tankers mentioned in Friday’s Guard statement were additional vessels or were among those involved in the incidents reported Thursday.U.S. Central Command disputes Iranian claimsAdm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz’s main shipping lanes had been cleared of Iranian naval mines.He also claimed that Iran’s navy had been destroyed and that Revolutionary Guard forces were no longer operating in the waterway.Cooper said U.S. forces remained in the region to keep major shipping routes open and secure.CENTCOM also rejected a claim made Thursday by the Revolutionary Guard that it had taken control of an American MQM-170 Outlaw drone in the western Strait of Hormuz.Iranian sources, meanwhile, reported Friday that an American unmanned surface vessel had been destroyed in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military had neither confirmed nor denied that report at the time of publication.The growing number of maritime incidents comes amid a continuing dispute between Washington and Tehran over the routes used by commercial shipping through the strategic waterway.Iran has demanded that vessels coordinate their movements with Iranian authorities and use routes closer to the strait’s northern shores. Ships seeking to avoid Iranian control have instead used the southern route.Qatari mediators return to Tehran amid threats of renewed U.S. strikesDiplomatic efforts to prevent another major escalation in the U.S.-Iran war are continuing alongside mounting military tensions in the Strait of Hormuz.CBS News, citing a source familiar with the negotiations, reported signs of progress and said Iran was expected to respond to a revised proposal from Qatari mediators by the end of the week.The diplomatic initiative is aimed at preventing a resumption of large-scale U.S. strikes against Iran, a possibility President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised in recent weeks.Axios reported that Qatari-led mediators were seeking common ground on issues including inspections of Iran’s nuclear facilities and sanctions relief.However, disagreements persisted over the conditions for formally opening negotiations.Axios also reported that the United States and Israel were considering options for extensive military strikes against Iran after the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections.The Associated Press reported Thursday, citing two diplomats, that Washington had warned several regional allies about the possibility of renewed U.S. attacks on Iran and potential Iranian retaliation, although Trump had not made a final decision.Trump, speaking Friday to a Kansas City radio station, said the war with Iran would end "soon," but did not specify whether that would be achieved through a diplomatic agreement or military action.The U.S. president reiterated that Washington wanted guarantees that Iran would never acquire a nuclear weapon.His remarks came as there was still no clear indication that Tehran and Washington had reached an agreement on the conditions for ending the war, while the possibility of renewed large-scale military strikes remained on the table.
